Looking at the last formula, it still has two problems:

1. The `total_hunger <= F` branch computes `F·H_i/total_hunger`, which is **larger** than `H_i` whenever `F > total_hunger` — it over-allocates instead of just satisfying hunger.
2. More fundamentally, the piecewise `min(max(...))` clamping does **not** conserve the budget: after clamping, `Σ F_i ≠ F`. If some animals hit their minimum, the total handed out exceeds `F`; if some hit their maximum, food is left unallocated. Per-animal clamping can never fix this.

What you need is a *single* parameter that is solved for globally — the standard "constrained proportional allocation" / water-filling formula.

## Notation

For each animal `i` (with `S` the set of animals):

- `l_i = L_i` if a minimum is defined, else `0`
- `u_i = M_i` if a maximum is defined, else `+∞`

## The formula

\[
\boxed{\;F_i \;=\; \min\Bigl(\max\bigl(\lambda\,H_i,\; l_i\bigr),\; u_i\Bigr)\quad\text{for every } i,\;}
\]

where `λ` is the **single scalar** determined by the budget constraint

\[
\lambda \;=\; \min\Bigl\{\, \lambda \ge 0 \;:\; \sum_{i\in S} \min\bigl(\max(\lambda H_i, l_i), u_i\bigr) \;\ge\; F \,\Bigr\}.
\]

That is: the unique `λ` satisfying

\[
\sum_{i\in S} \min\bigl(\max(\lambda H_i, l_i), u_i\bigr) \;=\; F .
\]

Since the left-hand side is continuous and non-decreasing in `λ` (piecewise linear, slope `Σ_{i: l_i < λH_i < u_i} H_i ≥ 0`), `λ` exists, is unique when at least one animal is interior, and is found in a few iterations of bisection (or exactly by sorting animals on `l_i/H_i` and `u_i/H_i` and walking the breakpoints).

## Why this is the fair pro-rata rule

It is the exact solution of

\[
\min_{F_i}\ \sum_{i\in S} \frac{(F_i - H_i)^2}{H_i}
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_i F_i = F,\;\; l_i \le F_i \le u_i ,
\]

i.e. the weighted (by hunger) projection of the hunger vector onto the feasible budget set. KKT gives `F_i = H_i(1-\mu)` clamped to `[l_i, u_i]`, which is precisely the formula above with `λ = 1-μ`. So:

- `λ = 1` ⇒ everyone exactly at hunger (`F = ΣH_i`);
- `λ < 1` ⇒ shortage is shared **pro-rata to hunger**, subject to floors/ceilings;
- `λ > 1` ⇒ surplus, only used to lift animals whose minimum exceeds their hunger.

No case analysis on which thresholds exist is needed — missing thresholds are absorbed by `l_i = 0` / `u_i = +∞`.

## Infeasible cases (must be stated)

The clamping formula is only defined when the budget is reachable:

\[
\sum_i l_i \;\le\; F \;\le\; \sum_i u_i .
\]

- **`F < Σ l_i`** (total minimums exceed the food): the constraints are inconsistent — no allocation respects all minimums. The only fair resolution is to ration the minimums proportionally:
  \[
  F_i = l_i \cdot \frac{F}{\sum_j l_j},
  \]
  and report that minimums cannot be honoured.
- **`F > Σ u_i`** (total maximums below the food): set `F_i = u_i` for all `i`; the surplus `F - Σ u_i` is unallocatable under the caps.
- If you also want to forbid over-feeding, use `u_i = min(M_i, H_i)`; then a large `F` simply leaves a surplus.

Sanity check: by construction `Σ F_i = F` whenever `Σ l_i ≤ F ≤ Σ u_i`, which the earlier answers never guaranteed.

Your instinct is right, but the list above mixes in some errors — and it misses the answer you're probably looking for.

**Corrections first:**
- The **Anglo-Irish Treaty was 1921**, not 1971 (it created the Irish Free State).
- **SALT I was signed in 1972** (May 1972, alongside the ABM Treaty); 1971 was the year of the SALT talks and the Hotline/ABM agreements, not the treaty signing.
- The **"UN declared zip codes worldwide"** item is not real.
- Bangladesh's independence (Dec 1971) and *Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg* (April 1971) and the Intel 4004 (late 1971) are accurate.

**The 1971 event that actually explains "charts deviating from the norm":**

On **August 15, 1971**, Nixon closed the gold window — ending dollar convertibility to gold and effectively dissolving the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates. This is the single most consequential "regime break" of the postwar era, and many long-run charts do visibly kink around 1971–73:

- **Currencies** go from flat peg lines to floating, volatile series.
- **Gold** breaks from its fixed $35/oz anchor and begins its long climb.
- **US trade balance** flips from surplus to persistent deficit.
- **Real wages vs. productivity** — the two lines tracked together from the 1940s, then split apart in the early 1970s.
- **Inflation and interest rates** become volatile and upward-drifting (the "Great Inflation"), breaking the stable post-war Phillips curve relationship.
- **Productivity growth** slows sharply after 1973.
- **Oil** is hit by the 1973 embargo, partly a consequence of the new monetary/exchange-rate environment.
- **Corporate profits' share of GDP, union density, and household debt** all show trend changes in this window.

Caveat: 1971 isn't magic on its own. The break is really a cluster — Bretton Woods' collapse (1971), the oil shocks (1973, 1979), the shift to floating rates (1973), and the productivity slowdown — so attributing a given chart to "1971" specifically is often a coincidence of dates rather than causation. If you tell me *which* charts you're looking at, I can be much more specific about the mechanism for each.

Happy to help. Here's a template based on your outline, plus notes on what makes the second email work.

## Template

**Subject:** SmartFit follow-up — a few questions on [Firm Name]'s investment focus

> Hi [Investor's Name],
>
> I'm following up on my earlier note after the Startup Grind panel in San Francisco, where I pitched SmartFit, our wearable fitness tracker. I know your inbox is crowded, so I'll keep this short.
>
> Before reaching out again, I spent some time with [Firm Name]'s portfolio and your writing on [specific thesis / portfolio company / talk]. It struck me that [one concrete point of alignment — e.g., "your focus on connected hardware with recurring revenue maps closely to our subscription attach rate of X%"]. I'd rather not assume we're a fit, though — I'd love to understand how you actually evaluate companies at our stage.
>
> A few things I'd find genuinely useful:
> - What are the key factors you weigh when evaluating a pre-Series A hardware startup?
> - Which metrics matter most to you — retention, unit economics, or growth rate?
> - What's your typical check size and level of involvement post-investment?
>
> Quick update on our side since the pitch: [1–2 concrete milestones — e.g., shipped to X users, signed a partnership with Y, grew MRR Z%]. Happy to send the latest one-pager if useful.
>
> Would a 20-minute call in the next couple of weeks work? I'm flexible [day/time options]. Either way, I appreciate the time you gave us at the panel.
>
> Best,
> [Your Name]
> [Title], SmartFit — [phone] · [LinkedIn]

## How to structure it well

- **Lead with the value of their time, not yours.** The line that makes a second email work is "here's what I did with your feedback / here's something specific I noticed about your firm." Generic flattery gets ignored.
- **Keep the ask small.** Three questions max, and make them answerable in a sentence. A long questionnaire reads like homework.
- **Put the questions in a bulleted list.** Investors often reply inline — make that easy.
- **One update, not five.** Pick the single most impressive, most verifiable milestone. Vague "significant progress" language actively hurts credibility.
- **Concrete time options beat "let me know when you're free."** Two specific windows get a yes or a counter-proposal.
- **Length:** 150–200 words total. If it doesn't fit on one phone screen, cut.

## Two cautions

1. **Don't ask for their criteria in a way that implies you'll contort the company to fit.** Frame it as "helping me figure out if this is worth your time," not "tell me what to say."
2. **If they don't reply to this one, stop emailing.** One follow-up after a pitch plus one substantive nudge is the limit; after that, a short note at a real milestone (new funding, big partnership, press) is the right re-entry point.

Yes — several of these have real sustainability programs worth checking:

1. **Patagonia** — the strongest of the group. Recycled nylon shells, 100% recycled down (from post-consumer garments) or responsibly sourced down, plus Worn Wear for repairs/resale.
2. **The North Face** — *Renewed* (professionally cleaned/refurbished returns) and garments using recycled down and recycled polyester; they also publish a sustainability/impact report per product.
3. **Columbia** — many jackets use recycled polyester shells and RDS-certified (Responsible Down Standard) down; look for their "Made With Recycled Content" callouts.
4. **Uniqlo** — *RE.UNIQLO*: recycled down jackets, repair/Re:Uniqlo studios in some stores, and the Ultra Light Down line uses RDS down.
5. **Eddie Bauer** — recycled down and recycled polyester in many styles, plus bluesign®-approved fabrics. **One correction to what I said earlier:** "Green Shape" is actually a Jack Wolfskin label, not Eddie Bauer's — sorry for the mix-up.

Two quick caveats:
- "Recycled" claims vary a lot; check the specific product's materials list rather than the brand page, and look for third-party certification (RDS, bluesign®, GRS for recycled content).
- Plus-size availability tends to be thinnest in the most technical/eco lineups, so if a style you like doesn't come in your size, check the previous season's colorways — those often have extended sizes marked down.

answer:
It sounds like you're already on a really good track — and that tension you're feeling (wanting to be generous vs. wanting to protect your wallet) is extremely common. Here are a few ways to think about it that go a bit deeper than a checklist:

**Separate "appreciation" from "spending."**
They're two different currencies. Appreciation is expressed through attention — remembering what someone mentioned three months ago, timing a gift to a hard week, writing a note that references something specific. None of that costs money, and in practice it's what people actually remember. Your self-care package to your brother is a perfect example: the meaningful part was that you noticed he was struggling.

**Give your budget a number before you browse.**
Overspending usually happens in the browsing phase, not the deciding phase. Decide your total gift budget for the year (or the season), divide it by person/occasion, and write those numbers into the gift list you're already building. Then the list becomes a constraint rather than a wish list — you're shopping *against* a number, not browsing until something feels right.

**Use a "one-in, one-out" rule for online shopping generally.**
Since you mentioned the volume of online shopping is part of what's overwhelming you: a simple rule is nothing new gets ordered until something comparable leaves (used up, donated, or returned). It slows the reflex-click and makes each purchase deliberate.

**Watch for the "upgrade trap."**
The most common budget leak is upgrading a good idea. You find a $30 gift, then think "but for $45 it'd be *so* much better," then add gift wrap and expedited shipping. Set the per-person number and treat add-ons as part of it, not outside it.

**Have a tiered default.**
Pre-decide three price tiers — say a small "thinking of you" tier, a standard birthday/holiday tier, and a "big occasion" tier — and assign people to tiers once a year. Decisions made in advance are far cheaper than decisions made in a panic the week before.

**Let the calendar do the work.**
Spreading purchases out (and shopping sales for things you already know you need) is the single biggest lever. Last-minute shopping is where budgets die — expedited shipping and full-price panic buys.

**Track spending where you already are.**
You don't need new software. An extra column in the gift list — budgeted, actual, difference — gives you a running total you'll actually look at, unlike a separate receipts app you'll forget.

**Give yourself a "no-guilt" allowance.**
Budget a small guilt-free amount each month for spontaneous generosity. Paradoxically, having a defined pot to spend freely on others makes it much easier to say no the rest of the time.

One reframe that helps: being financially steady *is* part of caring for the people you love. A gift that strains your budget creates its own quiet stress, and the people close to you would rather have you calm and present than stretched thin.

Want to sketch out actual numbers — a rough annual gift budget and how you'd split it across occasions? That's usually the step that turns these ideas into something usable.

That's a great question to end on — and I think your own reading list answers it.

I'd say historical fiction resonates for a few overlapping reasons:

- **It makes the abstract personal.** "The Nightingale" doesn't teach you the statistics of occupied France; it makes you feel the ration lines, the fear at curfew, the cost of a single lie. History becomes a lived experience rather than a date.
- **Distance creates safety to confront hard things.** Reading about sacrifice, complicity, or courage in another era gives us emotional room to reflect on those same impulses in ourselves — and in the present.
- **The recognition of continuity.** Ordinary people in the past loved, worried, and hoped much as we do. That bridge is oddly comforting.
- **Strong characters, not just settings.** What you loved in Vianne and Isabelle — the sisterly bond, the resilience — is what makes the history stick. Good historical fiction is character-driven first.
- **And a bit of mystery: the gaps.** Novels can fill the silences the record leaves behind — especially women's lives, which is exactly what "The Nightingale" and "The Alice Network" do.

Given how much the *relationships* mattered to you in "The Nightingale," I suspect that's your real draw — the history is the pressure that reveals the characters.

I've made a note of your reading tastes and plans (starting "The Alice Network," audiobooks for morning runs, Goodreads + your Book Lover's Journal, and book chats with Rachel), so we can pick this up easily next time. Happy reading — and enjoy Quinn!

answer:
Yes — here are the main reform proposals that come up, grouped by the structural problem they target:

**Senate floor / minority leverage**
- **Filibuster reform:** abolish it, or shift from a 60-vote cloture requirement to a "talking filibuster" (sustained floor debate instead of mere objection), or carve out exceptions (as already done for judicial nominees and some budget items via reconciliation).
- **Cloture reform:** shorten the 30-hour post-cloture debate window that still slows business.
- **Holds reform:** limit the ability of a single senator to anonymously stall nominations and bills.

**Committee bottlenecks**
- Time limits on committee consideration, or automatic discharge of bills that sit idle; streamlining subcommittee layers.
- Reviving regular order — more open amendment and floor debate in the Senate, where leaders increasingly negotiate mega-packages behind closed doors.

**House-side changes**
- Open rules vs. structured rules: proposals to guarantee minority-party amendments, so the majority can't entirely exclude the other side (relevant to the "Hastert rule" practice of only bringing up bills with majority-party support).
- Multi-member districts / ranked-choice voting: meant to reduce polarization and create incentives to compromise.

**Districting and elections**
- Independent redistricting commissions instead of partisan gerrymandering; some proposals tie this to voting-rights legislation.
- Campaign finance disclosure and lobbying transparency rules — the theory being that voters can then reward compromise.

**Process and calendar**
- Biennial budgeting and fixed appropriations deadlines to reduce reliance on omnibus packages and continuing resolutions.
- "Fast-track" or expedited procedures for specific categories (trade promotion authority and reconciliation are existing examples).

**Why these mostly stall:** each change alters the balance of power, so the current majority has little incentive to weaken tools it may soon need in the minority. Most reforms also require the very supermajorities or cross-chamber agreement they're designed to avoid — which is why the biggest real-world changes (nuclear option, reconciliation use, blue-slip limits) have come from one party acting unilaterally rather than from bipartisan reform.
